Volume 07 · Chapter 07

Taxes, accruals and earnings quality

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c06

By the endIdentify timing differences and assess sustainability of reported earnings.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can reconcile accounting profit, taxable profit, tax expense and cash tax; trace temporary differences through their reversal; and assess whether reported earnings provide a useful basis for a decision. Retain the three-statement identities, working-capital bridges, asset carrying amounts and equity and reporting-entity boundaries. A tax charge belongs to a specified company, jurisdiction and period: consolidated profit is not automatically one taxable base.

All companies, rules, rates and numbers below are original instructional constructions. Amounts are kCU, thousands of fictional currency units, unless CU is stated. The main case uses two fictional years and an expressly supplied tax law. It is neither a tax return nor a claim that a real jurisdiction permits these deductions. The cited public IAS 12 overview, dated Australian issuer texts and U.S. SEC staff interpretations establish narrowly identified concepts; they do not establish universal reporting compliance.

1. Four tax numbers can all be correct

Profit before tax, P, follows the case's financial-accounting recognition rules. Taxable profit, T, follows its tax rules. Current tax C is the resulting current-period charge. Cash tax, K, is the amount paid: installments, old balances or overpayments can make it differ from C. Deferred tax accounts for specified future tax consequences of amounts already recognized. It is not a second current tax bill.

The IFRS Foundation's public IAS 12 overview distinguishes unpaid current tax, overpayments and deferred tax, and notes recognition conditions and exceptions. It also identifies the reporting-date enacted or substantively enacted law as relevant to current measurement. We assume the fictional law below is already enacted; a hoped-for tax reduction is not one of its inputs.

Let LC be current tax payable, DTL a deferred tax liability and DTA a recognized deferred tax asset. In a simple case with all tax changes in profit, no acquisitions, currency translation, tax credits, refunds, equity/other-comprehensive-income tax effects or other movements:

Closing LC = opening LC + C − K.
Deferred tax expense ED = ΔDTL − ΔDTA.
Total tax expense ET = C + ED.
Net income NI = P − ET.

A growing DTL produces expense in this restricted bridge; a growing recognized DTA produces a benefit. A reduction reverses the sign. These equations cannot be carried unchanged into a group acquisition or an item whose tax effect belongs outside profit. Nor does an increase in a tax asset mean that cash has arrived.

For example, current tax payable opening at 6, a charge of 14 and payments of 15 leave a payable of 5. If DTL rises 5 while DTA rises 3, deferred expense is 2 and total tax expense is 16. Payment of 15 and expense of 16 differ by the payable change −1 plus deferred expense 2. No missing cash needs to be invented to reconcile them.

2. Tax bases identify future consequences

The carrying amount is the accounting balance. The tax base describes the amount assigned under the tax rules for recovering an asset or settling a liability. A temporary difference links those two measurements. A permanent difference affects accounting and tax differently without a later reversing deduction or taxable amount.

The September 2023 AASB 112 compilation, paragraphs 7–8, defines the asset tax base using future deductible recovery amounts and the liability tax base using future settlement deductions, with a separate advance-revenue rule. Paragraphs 24–36 condition DTA recognition on usable taxable profit; paragraphs 47 and 53 address applicable future rates and no discounting. Our cases exclude the standard's exceptions and apply these specified conditions directly.

Directions under the chapter's positive-rate, ordinary recovery/settlement assumptions
ItemDifferenceConsequence if recognized
AssetCarrying amount exceeds tax baseTaxable temporary difference; DTL
AssetTax base exceeds carrying amountDeductible temporary difference; possible DTA
Ordinary liabilityCarrying amount exceeds tax base because settlement is deductible laterDeductible temporary difference; possible DTA
EitherEqual amounts with no other tax consequenceNo temporary difference from that balance

To understand the asset direction, consider an amount of productive equipment still recorded at 30 but with only 10 of future deductions. Recovering 30 while deducting 10 leaves 20 exposed to tax in the stipulated model. At 20%, the associated DTL is 4. This is a conditional calculation about recovery, not evidence that the equipment could actually be sold for 30.

For a repair obligation of 12 deductible only when paid, the liability tax base is 12 − 12 = 0. Settlement consumes cash but creates a future deduction of 12. At 20%, a fully recoverable DTA is 2.4. A fine payable of 4 that is never deductible has tax base 4 − 0 = 4; its balance creates no DTA. Writing “all unpaid expenses create tax assets” would therefore be wrong.

DTA is not “deduction times rate” without a recognition assessment. The company needs usable taxable resources in the right entity, tax category and time window, considering relevant reversal and expiry rules. In a stipulated case with a deduction of 18 expiring next year, certain usable taxable income of only 8, no other taxable reversals and no carryforward, a 20% rate supports only 1.6, not 3.6. The remaining potential benefit cannot reduce tax on income that does not exist. A forecast supporting the 8 is evidence to scrutinize; the arithmetic does not create it.

3. Follow an entire temporary difference, including settlement

Worked example 1 — Northstar's two-year tax, profit and cash reconciliation

Northstar Calibration receives equity cash of 100 at date 0 and immediately buys equipment for 60. It has cash 40 and equipment 60, with no liabilities. The equipment is ready immediately, has zero residual and is fully consumed over two years. Book depreciation is 30 each year; the fictional tax deductions are 50 in year 1 and 10 in year 2. There is no sale, impairment or further investment.

Year 1 service revenue of 210 is earned and collected; ordinary expense of 105 is incurred and paid. A paid fine of 5 is an accounting expense and is permanently nondeductible under the supplied law. Existing completed service contracts create a supported repair obligation of 12, recognized as expense but paid entirely in year 2. In year 2, revenue and ordinary cash expense are 180 and 110; repair cash is exactly 12, with no new obligation. All other balances and transactions are absent.

The tax rate is 20% in both years. Ordinary revenue/expense follow the same timing for book and tax; repairs are deducted only when paid. Full DTA recognition is supported by sufficient future taxable resources, already evidenced at year 1 close. Current tax cash paid in year 1 is 8; year 2 pays its entire current charge and the remaining year 1 payable. Tax cash is operating. Gross DTA and DTL are displayed for teaching; no real offset eligibility is asserted.

Northstar's performance and tax bridge, kCU
MeasureYear 1Year 2
Book profit before tax210 − 105 − 5 − 30 − 12 = 58180 − 110 − 30 = 40
Taxable profit210 − 105 − 50 = 55180 − 110 − 10 − 12 = 48
Current tax charge119.6
Tax cash paid / closing payable8 / 312.6 / 0
Equipment carrying amount / tax base30 / 100 / 0
Repair provision / its tax base12 / 00 / 0
Closing DTL / DTA4 / 2.40 / 0
Deferred tax expense4 − 2.4 = 1.6−4 − (−2.4) = −1.6
Total tax expense / net income12.6 / 45.48 / 32

The year 1 book-to-tax bridge is 58 + 5 + 12 + 30 − 50 = 55: add back the nondeductible fine, the unpaid repair expense and book depreciation, then deduct tax depreciation. In year 2 the repair settlement is not another book expense; it is a tax deduction. Thus 40 + 30 − 10 − 12 = 48. Treating the payment as a new book expense would count the same obligation twice.

Year 1 tax entries are Dr Current tax expense 11 / Cr Current tax payable 11, followed by Dr Payable 8 / Cr Cash 8. Record Dr Deferred tax expense 4 / Cr DTL 4 and Dr DTA 2.4 / Cr Deferred tax benefit 2.4. Their net deferred charge is 1.6. The repair entry is Dr Repair expense 12 / Cr Provision 12. In year 2, Dr Provision 12 / Cr Cash 12 settles it, and both deferred balances reverse. The year 2 current charge 9.6 plus the opening payable 3 explains payment 12.6.

Direct year 1 CFO is 210 − 105 − 5 − 8 = 92; cash closes at 132. Assets are cash 132 + equipment 30 + DTA 2.4 = 164.4. Liabilities are provision 12 + current tax payable 3 + DTL 4 = 19. Equity is 100 + 45.4 = 145.4. Thus 164.4 = 19 + 145.4.

Year 2 CFO is 180 − 110 − 12 − 12.6 = 45.4. Cash closes at 177.4. Equipment, provision and all tax balances are zero, so cash is the only asset, liabilities are zero and equity is 145.4 + 32 = 177.4. Lifetime tax cash and expense both equal 20.6. Lifetime net income is 77.4, also the final cash increase over the initial equity 100. Total CFO 137.4 less date-0 investment 60 gives the same 77.4.

Year 1's effective tax rate, defined here as total tax expense divided by positive PBT, is 12.6/58 ≈ 21.72%. The difference from 20% is the permanently nondeductible fine: 12.6 = 0.20(58 + 5). The 8 cash payment divided by profit is a different measure. A zero or negative PBT can make the expense-to-profit ratio unstable or misleading; explain the amounts before interpreting the percentage.

4. Derive the operating-cash bridge

In Northstar, let B be book depreciation, W expense for the repair obligation, S its cash settlement and Q its provision balance. ΔQ = W − S. Current tax payable changes by C − K. Starting with NI and undoing each noncash or differently timed item gives:

CFO = NI + B + ΔQ + ED + ΔLC.
Year 1: 45.4 + 30 + 12 + 1.6 + 3 = 92.
Year 2: 32 + 30 − 12 − 1.6 − 3 = 45.4.

Substitute NI = revenue − ordinary expense − fine − B − W − C − ED. The added terms cancel B and ED, replace W with S and replace C with K. What remains is precisely the cash ledger. This derivation explains the signs rather than memorizing an addback list.

A deferred benefit is negative expense, so undoing it subtracts from NI in the cash bridge. A provision payment reduces cash even if the expense was recorded earlier. An unpaid current tax charge temporarily retains cash. If there are also receivables, inventory and payables, add their correctly defined operating movements from Chapter 3, excluding movements already represented here. Do not include a tax payable once in generic payables and again in its own line.

5. An estimate is a claim about evidence

A provision is a recognized obligation with uncertainty about its amount or timing; an ordinary accrued payable generally involves less uncertainty. Under the dated AASB 137 compilation, recognition requires a present obligation from a past event, probable outflow and a reliable estimate. A management plan for future operating expenditure is insufficient. Contingent liabilities have different recognition/disclosure treatment. Estimates require reassessment; uncertain obligations do not justify arbitrary excess reserves. Material time value calls for discounting, and subsequent settlement uses the provision for its original purpose. These are selected boundaries, not the complete standard.

For Northstar, the obligation comes from services already delivered with a contractual assurance obligation; the supplied evidence supports 12 of expected settlement cost. Calling a desired profit reduction a “reserve” would not establish a liability. Conversely, failing to recognize an evidenced obligation would overstate current profit. A provision liability is also different from Chapter 3's receivable allowance, which reduces an asset.

Worked example 2 — A higher reserve shifts earnings; evidence decides whether it is justified

Hold every Northstar cash event and tax rule fixed. Suppose year 1 repair expense and provision are recorded as 20, with full recognition of the associated DTA, while actual year 2 settlement remains 12. We are comparing estimates, not adding eight of actual repairs. In year 1 PBT falls from 58 to 50. Taxable profit and current tax remain 55 and 11 because neither estimate is currently deductible. DTA becomes 4, matching DTL 4, so deferred expense is zero. NI is 39, lower by 6.4. Cash remains 132.

In year 2 the 20 provision exceeds actual settlement by 8. Settlement and release together are Dr Provision 20 / Cr Cash 12 / Cr Repair-expense reversal 8. PBT becomes 48; current tax is still 9.6. Both equal deferred balances disappear, leaving net deferred expense zero and NI 38.4, higher by 6.4. Lifetime NI remains 77.4; tax cash and operating cash in both years are unchanged. The year 1 increase of eight in expense becomes a later eight of pretax relief.

That pattern can result from an honest estimate followed by favorable news, an avoidable estimation error, or an intentionally inflated initial reserve. The two financial statements alone do not identify which explanation is true. Compare information actually available at each reporting date: claim histories, repair-cost studies, contract terms, engineering changes and subsequent claim outcomes. A hindsight observation of twelve does not prove that twenty was unreasonable when estimated; an unsupported twenty is not justified merely because it will eventually reverse.

The temptation is clear when compensation rewards a later profit target, management changes after a bad year, or a covenant uses reported earnings. Controls should make the assumptions, approval and subsequent outcomes visible. Evaluate estimate accuracy across many periods and both favorable and unfavorable revisions; do not judge only whether one quarter met its target.

A different example isolates discounting. If a qualifying obligation requires a certain 121 cash settlement in two years and a consistent 10% discount rate is supplied, its initial amount is 121/1.1² = 100. After one year with unchanged expectations and no payment, it is 110. The increase of ten reflects time, not another accident or cash transfer. Tax effects are excluded from this separate example; a discounted provision and an undiscounted deferred tax balance need not use the same measurement convention.

6. Earnings quality depends on the question

A useful earnings measure should describe the company's performance under a clear definition and provide evidence relevant to forecasting or stewardship. Examine whether transactions occurred, estimates are supported, policies are applied consistently, unusual items are explained, and profit converts into cash on a plausible operating schedule. None of these questions is answered by one ratio.

Accrual accounting can improve measurement: delivering goods creates a claim even before collection, and a repair obligation is a cost even before payment. Accruals are therefore not inherently suspect. Problems arise when recognition lacks evidence, estimates are opportunistic or an analyst mistakes a timing effect for sustainable operating improvement. Cash also needs interpretation: delayed supplier payments or tax installments can raise current CFO while leaving an obligation for later.

Worked example 3 — Cash conversion and selective adjustments

Two separate companies have no tax or other noncash differences beyond those supplied. Company A reports NI 80 and depreciation 20; receivables rise 45, inventory rises 15 and operating payables rise 10. CFO is 80 + 20 − 45 − 15 + 10 = 50. Company B reports NI 65 and depreciation 20; receivables rise 5, inventory is unchanged and payables fall 5. CFO is 65 + 20 − 5 − 5 = 75.

A has higher profit and lower cash flow. The gap could reflect profitable growth on ordinary credit, slower collections, more inventory or improper revenue recognition. To distinguish them, inspect volumes/prices, invoice dates, contractual terms, aging, later collections, returns and stock movements. B's supplied working-capital movements also absorb cash: the receivable increase and payable decline use ten. Its depreciation addback of twenty more than offsets that absorption, explaining why CFO exceeds NI. These figures alone do not identify either company's growth trajectory. With beginning assets of 500 each, the simple accrual measure (NI − CFO)/beginning assets is 6% for A and −2% for B. It summarizes the gap; it does not assign a probability of fraud.

Now consider an unrelated company's PBT of 40, including an isolated disposal gain of 12, a release of an old provision of 6, restructuring expense of 8 and a currency loss of 4. Management adds back the last two items and calls 52 “underlying profit,” retaining both gains. If the analyst's explicit comparison excludes the isolated gain and old-estimate release but retains recurring restructuring and currency exposure, the result is 22. If credible evidence instead supports a normal restructuring cost of 5, replace the actual 8 with 5 to obtain 25. The difference reflects an assumption that must be defended; neither 22 nor 25 is newly generated cash.

The SEC staff's non-GAAP interpretations, questions 100.01–100.06, discuss recurring operating costs, consistency, asymmetric removal of losses and gains, altered recognition and misleading labels. These U.S. staff interpretations are a useful warning against selective adjustments, not authority that our fictional analytical measure satisfies every disclosure rule. Reconcile each adjustment, state its purpose, treat comparable gains and losses consistently, and show evidence for recurrence assumptions.

“Noncash” does not mean “without economic cost.” Depreciation allocates resources consumed; equity compensation can pay for employee services through ownership claims; a credit loss can destroy a valuable receivable. Removing all such costs may make a number larger while making it less useful. Likewise, a nonrecurring item can still consume cash and reduce wealth. Keep the historical reconciliation visible even when constructing a forward-looking measure.

When presenting a diagnosis, state the observation, competing mechanisms, evidence that would distinguish them, and the decision sensitive to the uncertainty. For example: “Receivables grew faster than credit sales; the cause is unresolved. Test delivery cutoff and subsequent collections before extrapolating the margin.” That is more informative than either declaring fraud or accepting management's preferred adjusted number.

7. Reproduce the tax and provision model

Download the original inputs, standard-library analysis and guide together. Run python3 v07-c07-analysis.py. Exact fractions preserve both years' tax, cash, asset, provision and equity reconciliations. The program does not select a real tax rule, establish recoverability or assess documentary evidence.

Before changing an input, predict the consequences. Increase the year 1 estimate while keeping settlement fixed; accelerate book depreciation while leaving tax deductions unchanged; change year 1 tax installments; or supply an enacted 25% year 2 rate. Identify which change alters current profit, actual cash timing, total cash or only the allocation of income between periods. The model deliberately rejects tax losses, incomplete depreciation schedules, insufficient supplied deduction capacity and implicit financing; extending those cases requires teaching their additional rules.

Exercises

Use the chapter's stated conventions. Amounts are kCU unless indicated. No unlisted transactions, tax effects outside profit or additional tax-law exceptions apply.

  1. Expense, charge and payment. Opening current tax payable is 6, current tax expense 14 and tax cash paid 15. DTL increases 5 and recognized DTA increases 3. PBT is 70. Find closing payable, deferred and total tax expense, NI, and the reconciliation of tax expense to cash paid. Explain why cash payment is not the tax expense.
  2. Tax bases and signs. At a supplied 20% rate, an asset has carrying amount 90 and future deductible tax base 60. A receivable of 20 has already been taxed and its future collection has no further tax effect. A repair liability of 15 will be fully deductible on payment; a fine liability of 4 will never be deductible. Determine each tax base and temporary difference, then gross DTL and recognized DTA assuming full recoverability. Does a net difference authorize offset in a real statement?
  3. Change book allocation only. In Northstar, replace book depreciation 30/30 with 40/20. Keep cash, tax depreciation, repairs, rates and tax installments unchanged. Find each year's PBT, DTA/DTL, deferred tax expense, total tax expense and NI; verify CFO and final equity. What changes if an analyst incorrectly treats the extra first-year depreciation as an additional cash payment?
  4. Obligation versus intention. Ignore tax. A board plans next year's marketing campaign costing 4 but can cancel it without penalty and has created no obligation to anyone. Separately, a qualifying existing obligation will require a certain 121 in two years; the supplied consistent discount rate is 10%. Determine the initial provision for each item and the second item's balance after one year with no payment or new information. Explain why the time-related increase is not a cash outflow or a new damaging event.
  5. A tax benefit needs usable income. A deductible temporary difference of 18 reverses next year. It expires unused to the extent it cannot offset that year's taxable income; there is no carryforward, other taxable reversal or planning opportunity. The supplied supported taxable capacity before the deduction is 8 and the tax rate 20%. Find the recognized DTA and unrecognized potential benefit. At a later reporting date, before reversal, new credible evidence raises capacity to 14 with all else unchanged. Find the revised DTA and effect on profit and cash. Explain why the improved forecast itself still needs evidence.
  6. Enacted future rate. Return to baseline Northstar. The year 1 current rate remains 20%, but a 25% year 2 rate is already enacted at year 1 close. Keep all cash events other than the resulting tax payments unchanged; year 1 tax cash remains 8. Find both year-end deferred balances, both years' total tax expense and NI, cash tax, CFO and final cash/equity. Separate year 1 remeasurement from the later cash effect.
  7. Build and defend an adjustment. A separate company reports PBT 36. It includes an isolated asset-sale gain 9, a litigation charge 7 for a documented settled one-time dispute, restructuring expense 4 that has recurred for three years and employee share-based compensation 6 for continuing services. Management adds all three expenses back, retaining the gain. Calculate management's adjusted number and a consistently defined comparison excluding only the isolated sale and dispute. Give two evidence checks that could change your normalization and explain why neither number can be called cash flow.
  8. Find the reconciliation error before judging intent. NI is 100, depreciation 25, receivables increase 60, inventory increases 20 and operating payables increase 15. With no other items, an analyst reports CFO 180 by adding the receivable increase. Reconstruct CFO and quantify the error. Give two plausible economic explanations for the correct cash/profit gap and the evidence distinguishing them. Then add a newly recognized DTA benefit of 10 that raises NI to 110 with no current tax or cash change; rebuild the cash bridge.
Complete solutions
  1. Closing current payable is 6 + 14 − 15 = 5. Deferred expense is 5 − 3 = 2; total expense is 16; NI is 70 − 16 = 54. Expense less cash is 16 − 15 = 1, equal to Δpayable −1 plus deferred expense 2. The payment settles some previously recorded tax as well as current obligations, while deferred tax changes recognized future consequences without current cash settlement.
  2. The asset tax base is 60; the taxable difference 90 − 60 = 30 produces DTL 6. The receivable tax base is 20 and its difference zero. The repair liability tax base is 15 − 15 = 0; the deductible difference 15 produces DTA 3. The fine liability tax base is 4 − 0 = 4 and produces no temporary difference. Gross DTL is 6 and DTA 3. Their arithmetic net is a liability of 3, but real offset depends on the applicable conditions, which this exercise does not establish. A permanent fine is not transformed into a future tax saving by remaining unpaid.
  3. Year 1 PBT is 48. Carrying amount is 20 versus tax base 10, so DTL is 2; DTA remains 2.4. Deferred expense is −0.4, current tax remains 11, total tax expense is 10.6 and NI is 37.4. Year 2 PBT is 50; both deferred balances become zero, giving deferred expense 0.4. Current tax 9.6 plus 0.4 gives total expense 10 and NI 40. CFO remains 37.4 + 40 + 12 − 0.4 + 3 = 92 and 40 + 20 − 12 + 0.4 − 3 = 45.4. Final equity remains 177.4. Treating the additional book charge 10 as extra cash would understate first-year cash/CFO by 10; the actual equipment payment already occurred at date 0. The after-tax profit shift is 8, not an extra resource payment.
  4. The cancelable campaign creates no provision under the stated facts; a budget is not an existing obligation. The separate qualifying obligation is initially 100, since 121/1.1² = 100. After one year it is 110, giving a time-related expense of 10 with cash zero. The balance then accumulates another 11 before settlement at 121. This is the supplied discounted measurement through time; no new incident or revised settlement estimate is needed to explain the increase.
  5. Only 8 of the deduction can be used, so recognized DTA is 0.20×8 = 1.6. Maximum potential benefit is 3.6, leaving 2 unrecognized. With capacity 14 the recognized amount becomes 2.8; the increase 1.2 is a tax benefit that raises current profit under the stated all-effects-in-profit convention. It changes current cash by zero. The remaining potential benefit is 0.8. Check the source of future taxable income, timing, expiry and whether forecast deductions have been counted twice; changing a spreadsheet forecast does not itself create usable taxable profit.
  6. At year 1 close, DTL is 20×25% = 5 and DTA is 12×25% = 3. Net deferred expense is 2. Current tax remains 11, so total expense is 13 and NI 45. Payment stays 8, payable 3, CFO 92 and cash 132. Gross assets 132+30+3 = 165 equal liabilities 12+3+5 = 20 plus equity 145. Year 2 current tax is 48×25% = 12; deferred expense is −5−(−3) = −2; total expense is 10 and NI 30. Tax cash is 3+12 = 15; CFO is 180−110−12−15 = 43; final cash/equity is 175. Compared with baseline, year 1 profit falls 0.4 without a cash change, then year 2 tax cash rises 2.4. The lifetime tax increase is 2.4; do not count the first-year remeasurement again as a separate payment.
  7. Management reports 36+7+4+6 = 53. The stated consistent comparison is 36−9+7 = 34: remove the isolated gain and expense while retaining recurring restructuring and continuing employee compensation. Evidence checks include whether similar disputes recur despite the label, whether restructuring reflects a continuing business strategy, whether sale gains are part of ordinary operations, and whether the compensation is needed to retain staff. A defensible answer specifies which evidence would change which adjustment and uses comparable treatment across periods. Neither result reconciles working capital, noncash charges, investment or financing; neither is CFO. Services paid through shares can have an economic cost even without a cash payment.
  8. Correct CFO is 100+25−60−20+15 = 60. Replacing −60 with +60 creates an error of 120, explaining the reported 180. Legitimate growth on credit and delayed/distressed customer collections can both create receivables growth; inspect credit sales, terms, aging and subsequent receipts. Inventory buildup can reflect planned demand or unsold stock; inspect dated stock movements and realizable demand. An arithmetic sign error does not by itself establish deliberate misreporting. With the DTA benefit, NI becomes 110 and deferred expense is −10; CFO is 110+25−60−20+15−10 = 60. The recognized tax asset has not collected cash.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back. Explain to a manager why Northstar reports year 1 tax expense 12.6, current tax 11 and cash tax 8, and why a larger repair estimate can lower this year's earnings without lowering cash.

Teach-back benchmark

Start with book profit 58 and the specified adjustments to taxable profit 55. Current tax is 11; installments 8 leave a payable of 3. Equipment's future taxable difference creates DTL 4 and the supported future repair deduction creates DTA 2.4, so net deferred expense is 1.6 and total expense 12.6. The repair estimate is not currently deductible or paid; increasing it changes book expense and DTA, then reverses through later settlement/reassessment. Its credibility depends on reporting-date evidence, not on balancing the journal.

Delayed check, one week later. Keep baseline Northstar's transactions and tax rates but pay all 11 of year 1 current tax in that year. Compute each year's tax payable, CFO and cash, and state which profit figures change.

Delayed-check answer

Year 1 payable is zero, CFO is 210−105−5−11 = 89 and cash is 129. Year 2 pays only its current charge 9.6, so CFO is 180−110−12−9.6 = 48.4 and cash is 177.4. Payable is zero at both closes. NI remains 45.4 and 32; all deferred balances and expenses are unchanged. The payment schedule transfers three of cash outflow from year 2 to year 1 without changing total tax or profit. A real taxpayer would need lawful payment terms; these are supplied fictional timing alternatives.

Continue to managerial accounting and cost decisions. Preserve the distinction between reported expense, an economically relevant incremental cost and a dated cash payment before choosing a business action.

Sources and further study

  • IFRS Foundation — IAS 12 Income Taxes, public overview — Current tax versus deferred tax, tax bases and conditions/exceptions; distinction between public overview and full normative text.
  • AASB 112 Income Taxes — September 2023 compilation — Scoped asset/liability tax-base definitions, usable-income condition for DTA recognition, future enacted rates, no discounting and allocation boundary.
  • AASB 137 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets — December 2022 compilation — Scoped provision versus accrual, present-obligation recognition, evidence, reassessment and discounting boundaries.
  • SEC Division of Corporation Finance — Non-GAAP Financial Measures staff interpretations — U.S.-specific staff cautions on recurring costs, consistency, removing gains as well as losses, altered recognition and clear labels.
